response: Yes, research suggests that elevated levels of asymmetric dimethylarginine (ADMA) in young adults born preterm may predict an early endothelial dysfunction. ADMA is an endogenous inhibitor of nitric oxide synthase, and high levels of ADMA have been associated with endothelial dysfunction, which is a precursor to cardiovascular disease. Studies have shown that individuals born preterm may have higher levels of ADMA and an increased risk of endothelial dysfunction, which could contribute to the development of cardiovascular disease later in life. Therefore, measuring ADMA levels in young adults born preterm may be a useful predictor of early endothelial dysfunction and potential cardiovascular risk.
